data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's position is inconsistent: he rejects induction logically but reinstates it biologically/psychologically as an unavoidable instinct for survival, making his system a descriptive account of scientific practice rather than a purely normative logic.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper can successfully separate the 'context of discovery' (psychological/biological) from the 'context of justification' (logical).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'preference' can be fully reconstructed as a logical imperative without appealing to biological instincts.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the biological explanation undermines the normative force of his own critical method.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Humans and scientists possess an innate tendency to expect regularities (induction) which evolution has hardwired for survival. Popper's 'preference' is an acknowledgment of this biological reality. While his logic forbids justifying induction, his philosophy of science describes how humans *actually* operate: we cannot help but act as if the future will resemble the past. The mechanism is 'evolutionary epistemology': we prefer corroborated theories because organisms that didn't would have died out. The cost is admitting that pure rationality (without inductive instinct) would lead to paralysis, and thus science rests on a non-rational, biological foundation.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
